## Part 1: Casting the Volterra System as a Linear Model via Kronecker Tensor Product

### 1.1 Input Vector and Kronecker Products

Define the **input snapshot vector** at time $t$ with memory order $M$:

$$\mathbf{x}(t, M) = \big[x(t),\; x(t-1),\; \ldots,\; x(t-M)\big]^T \in \mathbb{R}^{M+1}.$$

Define the **$k$-fold Kronecker product**:

$$\mathbf{x}^{[k]}(t, M) = \underbrace{\mathbf{x}(t,M) \otimes \mathbf{x}(t,M) \otimes \cdots \otimes \mathbf{x}(t,M)}_{k \text{ times}} \in \mathbb{R}^{(M+1)^k}.$$

By the definition of the Kronecker product, the entry of $\mathbf{x}^{[k]}(t,M)$ at the position indexed by the multi-index $(t_1, t_2, \ldots, t_k)$ with $t_i \in \{0, 1, \ldots, M\}$ is exactly

$$\big[\mathbf{x}^{[k]}(t,M)\big]_{(t_1,\ldots,t_k)} = \prod_{i=1}^{k} x(t - t_i).$$

### 1.2 Vectorizing the Volterra Kernel

Define $\mathbf{h}_{M,k} \in \mathbb{R}^{(M+1)^k}$ as the **vectorized $k$-th order Volterra kernel**, whose entries are $h_k(t_1, \ldots, t_k)$ arranged in the **same lexicographic order** as the entries of $\mathbf{x}^{[k]}(t, M)$. Then the $k$-th order Volterra contribution becomes an inner product:

$$\sum_{t_1, \ldots, t_k = 0}^{M} h_k(t_1, \ldots, t_k) \prod_{i=1}^{k} x(t - t_i) = \big[\mathbf{x}^{[k]}(t, M)\big]^T \mathbf{h}_{M,k}.$$

### 1.3 Assembling the Linear Model

Define the **data row vector** for the $k$-th order term:

$$\mathbf{D}_x(t, k, M) = \big[\mathbf{x}^{[k]}(t, M)\big]^T \in \mathbb{R}^{1 \times (M+1)^k}.$$

Stacking all $p$ orders, define the **combined parameter vector** and **combined data row vector**:

$$\mathbf{g}_M = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{h}_{M,1} \\ \mathbf{h}_{M,2} \\ \vdots \\ \mathbf{h}_{M,p} \end{bmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^{N(M)}, \qquad \mathbf{D}_x(t, M) = \big[\mathbf{D}_x(t,1,M),\; \ldots,\; \mathbf{D}_x(t,p,M)\big] \in \mathbb{R}^{1 \times N(M)},$$

where $N(M) = \sum_{k=1}^{p} (M+1)^k$ is the total number of parameters.

Collecting data over $s = 1, \ldots, t$, the **batch data matrix** is:

$$\mathbf{D}_x(t, M) = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{D}_x(1, M) \\ \mathbf{D}_x(2, M) \\ \vdots \\ \mathbf{D}_x(t, M) \end{bmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^{t \times N(M)}, \qquad \mathbf{y}_t = \begin{bmatrix} y(1) \\ \vdots \\ y(t) \end{bmatrix}, \quad \mathbf{e}_t = \begin{bmatrix} e(1) \\ \vdots \\ e(t) \end{bmatrix}.$$

The Volterra system is now cast as the **linear regression model**:

$$\boxed{\mathbf{y}_t = \mathbf{D}_x(t, M)\, \mathbf{g}_M + \mathbf{e}_t.}$$

Equivalently, at each time instant:

$$y(t) = \boldsymbol{\phi}^T(t, M)\, \mathbf{g}_M + e(t),$$

where $\boldsymbol{\phi}(t, M) = \mathbf{D}_x^T(t, M) = \big[\mathbf{x}^{[1]}(t,M)^T, \ldots, \mathbf{x}^{[p]}(t,M)^T\big]^T \in \mathbb{R}^{N(M)}$ is the **regressor vector**.

## Part 2: RLS Lattice Algorithm for Estimating $\mathbf{g}_M$

### 2.1 RLS Cost Function

The RLS estimate at time $t$, memory order $M$, minimizes the exponentially weighted least-squares cost:

$$J(t, M) = \sum_{s=1}^{t} \lambda^{t-s} \big[y(s) - \boldsymbol{\phi}^T(s, M)\, \hat{\mathbf{g}}_M(t)\big]^2, \qquad 0 < \lambda \leq 1,$$

where $\lambda$ is the **forgetting factor**. The solution is:

$$\hat{\mathbf{g}}_M(t) = \mathbf{R}_M^{-1}(t)\, \mathbf{p}_M(t),$$

with $\mathbf{R}_M(t) = \sum_{s=1}^{t} \lambda^{t-s} \boldsymbol{\phi}(s,M)\boldsymbol{\phi}^T(s,M)$ and $\mathbf{p}_M(t) = \sum_{s=1}^{t} \lambda^{t-s} \boldsymbol{\phi}(s,M)\, y(s)$.

### 2.2 Nested (Order-Recursive) Structure of the Regressor

The key property enabling the lattice is the **nested structure**: when $M \to M+1$, the input vector gains one component $x(t-M-1)$, and the Kronecker products grow accordingly. Specifically:

$$\mathbf{x}(t, M+1) = \big[\mathbf{x}(t,M)^T,\; x(t-M-1)\big]^T,$$

and the regressor decomposes as:

$$\boldsymbol{\phi}(t, M+1) = \begin{bmatrix} \boldsymbol{\phi}(t, M) \\ \boldsymbol{\zeta}(t, M+1) \end{bmatrix},$$

where $\boldsymbol{\zeta}(t, M+1) \in \mathbb{R}^{\Delta N(M)}$ collects **all new Kronecker product terms** involving $x(t-M-1)$. For each $k = 1, \ldots, p$, the new terms in $\mathbf{x}^{[k]}(t, M+1)$ are those products $\prod_{i=1}^k x(t - t_i)$ where at least one $t_i = M+1$. The dimension of the new block is:

$$\Delta N(M) = N(M+1) - N(M) = \sum_{k=1}^{p} \big[(M+2)^k - (M+1)^k\big].$$

### 2.3 Backward Prediction Errors — Orthogonal Basis

Define the **backward prediction error** at order $m$ ($m = 1, 2, \ldots, M$) as the residual of the new block $\boldsymbol{\zeta}(t, m)$ after projecting onto the existing regressor $\boldsymbol{\phi}(t, m-1)$:

$$\mathbf{b}_m(t) = \boldsymbol{\zeta}(t, m) - \mathbf{K}_m^T(t-1)\, \boldsymbol{\phi}(t, m-1) \in \mathbb{R}^{\Delta N(m-1)},$$

where $\mathbf{K}_m(t) \in \mathbb{R}^{N(m-1) \times \Delta N(m-1)}$ is the **backward prediction filter**:

$$\mathbf{K}_m(t) = \mathbf{R}_{m-1}^{-1}(t) \sum_{s=1}^{t} \lambda^{t-s} \boldsymbol{\phi}(s, m-1)\, \boldsymbol{\zeta}^T(s, m).$$

For the base case ($m = 0$): $\mathbf{b}_0(t) = \boldsymbol{\phi}(t, 0) = \big[x(t), x(t)^2, \ldots, x(t)^p\big]^T \in \mathbb{R}^p$.

**Orthogonality Property.** By construction (Gram–Schmidt orthogonalization in the exponentially weighted inner product $\langle \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \rangle_t = \sum_{s=1}^t \lambda^{t-s} \mathbf{u}^T(s) \mathbf{v}(s)$), the backward prediction errors satisfy:

$$\sum_{s=1}^{t} \lambda^{t-s}\, \mathbf{b}_i(s)\, \mathbf{b}_j^T(s) = \mathbf{0}, \qquad i \neq j.$$

Thus $\{\mathbf{b}_0(t), \mathbf{b}_1(t), \ldots, \mathbf{b}_M(t)\}$ forms an **orthogonal basis** for the column space of $\mathbf{D}_x(t, M)$.

### 2.4 Forward Prediction Errors

Define the **forward prediction error** at order $m$ as the residual of $\boldsymbol{\zeta}(t, m)$ after projecting onto the time-shifted regressor $\boldsymbol{\phi}(t-1, m-1)$:

$$\mathbf{f}_m(t) = \boldsymbol{\zeta}(t, m) - \mathbf{A}_m^T(t-1)\, \boldsymbol{\phi}(t-1, m-1) \in \mathbb{R}^{\Delta N(m-1)},$$

where $\mathbf{A}_m(t)$ is the **forward prediction filter**:

$$\mathbf{A}_m(t) = \mathbf{R}_{m-1}^{-1}(t-1) \sum_{s=1}^{t} \lambda^{t-s} \boldsymbol{\phi}(s-1, m-1)\, \boldsymbol{\zeta}^T(s, m).$$

### 2.5 Error Energy Matrices and Cross-Correlation

Define the **backward error energy matrix**:

$$\mathbf{E}_m^b(t) = \sum_{s=1}^{t} \lambda^{t-s}\, \mathbf{b}_m(s)\, \mathbf{b}_m^T(s) \in \mathbb{R}^{\Delta N(m-1) \times \Delta N(m-1)}.$$

Define the **forward error energy matrix**:

$$\mathbf{E}_m^f(t) = \sum_{s=1}^{t} \lambda^{t-s}\, \mathbf{f}_m(s)\, \mathbf{f}_m^T(s).$$

Define the **cross-correlation matrix** (capturing the temporal shift relationship):

$$\boldsymbol{\Delta}_m(t) = \sum_{s=1}^{t} \lambda^{t-s}\, \mathbf{f}_{m-1}(s)\, \mathbf{b}_{m-1}^T(s-1).$$

### 2.6 Reflection Coefficient Matrices

The **forward and backward reflection coefficient matrices** are:

$$\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_m^f(t) = \boldsymbol{\Delta}_m(t)\, \big[\mathbf{E}_{m-1}^b(t-1)\big]^{-1}, \qquad \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_m^b(t) = \boldsymbol{\Delta}_m^T(t)\, \big[\mathbf{E}_{m-1}^f(t)\big]^{-1}.$$

### 2.7 Order-Recursive (Lattice) Updates

The forward and backward prediction errors at order $m$ are related to those at order $m-1$ through the **lattice recursion**. Using the decomposition $\boldsymbol{\phi}(t-1, m-1) = [\boldsymbol{\phi}(t-1, m-2)^T, \boldsymbol{\zeta}(t-1, m-1)^T]^T$ and the orthogonality of $\mathbf{b}_{m-1}(t-1)$ to $\boldsymbol{\phi}(t-1, m-2)$, the projection of $\boldsymbol{\zeta}(t, m)$ onto $\boldsymbol{\phi}(t-1, m-1)$ decomposes into a projection onto $\boldsymbol{\phi}(t-1, m-2)$ plus a projection onto $\mathbf{b}_{m-1}(t-1)$. This yields:

$$\boxed{\mathbf{f}_m(t) = \mathbf{f}_{m-1}^{(m)}(t) - \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_m^f(t)\, \mathbf{b}_{m-1}(t-1),}$$

$$\boxed{\mathbf{b}_m(t) = \mathbf{b}_{m-1}^{(m)}(t) - \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_m^b(t)\, \mathbf{f}_{m-1}(t),}$$

where $\mathbf{f}_{m-1}^{(m)}(t)$ denotes the forward prediction error of $\boldsymbol{\zeta}(t,m)$ from $\boldsymbol{\phi}(t-1, m-2)$ alone, and $\mathbf{b}_{m-1}^{(m)}(t)$ denotes the backward prediction error of $\boldsymbol{\zeta}(t,m)$ from $\boldsymbol{\phi}(t, m-2)$ alone. These are the **block-lattice recursions** — the vector/matrix generalization of the scalar lattice.

### 2.8 Conversion Factor (Likelihood Variable)

Define the **conversion factor** $\gamma_m(t) \in (0, 1]$:

$$\gamma_0(t) = 1, \qquad \gamma_m(t) = \gamma_{m-1}(t) - \mathbf{b}_m^T(t)\, \big[\mathbf{E}_m^b(t)\big]^{-1}\, \mathbf{b}_m(t).$$

This relates **a priori** and **a posteriori** prediction errors:

$$\mathbf{b}_m(t) = \gamma_{m-1}(t)\, \boldsymbol{\beta}_m(t), \qquad \mathbf{f}_m(t) = \gamma_{m-1}(t-1)\, \boldsymbol{\eta}_m(t),$$

where $\boldsymbol{\beta}_m(t) = \boldsymbol{\zeta}(t,m) - \mathbf{K}_m^T(t-1)\boldsymbol{\phi}(t,m-1)$ and $\boldsymbol{\eta}_m(t) = \boldsymbol{\zeta}(t,m) - \mathbf{A}_m^T(t-1)\boldsymbol{\phi}(t-1,m-1)$ are the a priori errors.

### 2.9 Time-Recursive Updates

For each time step $t \to t+1$, the following quantities are updated for each order $m = 0, 1, \ldots, M$:

**(a) A priori backward prediction error:**
$$\boldsymbol{\beta}_m(t+1) = \boldsymbol{\zeta}(t+1, m) - \mathbf{K}_m^T(t)\, \boldsymbol{\phi}(t+1, m-1).$$

**(b) A posteriori backward prediction error:**
$$\mathbf{b}_m(t+1) = \gamma_{m-1}(t+1)\, \boldsymbol{\beta}_m(t+1).$$

**(c) Backward error energy:**
$$\mathbf{E}_m^b(t+1) = \lambda\, \mathbf{E}_m^b(t) + \mathbf{b}_m(t+1)\, \boldsymbol{\beta}_m^T(t+1).$$

**(d) Cross-correlation:**
$$\boldsymbol{\Delta}_m(t+1) = \lambda\, \boldsymbol{\Delta}_m(t) + \mathbf{f}_{m-1}(t+1)\, \mathbf{b}_{m-1}^T(t) / \gamma_{m-2}(t).$$

**(e) Reflection coefficients:**
$$\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_m^f(t+1) = \boldsymbol{\Delta}_m(t+1)\, \big[\mathbf{E}_{m-1}^b(t)\big]^{-1}, \qquad \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_m^b(t+1) = \boldsymbol{\Delta}_m^T(t+1)\, \big[\mathbf{E}_{m-1}^f(t+1)\big]^{-1}.$$

**(f) Conversion factor:**
$$\gamma_m(t+1) = \gamma_{m-1}(t+1) - \mathbf{b}_m^T(t+1)\, \big[\mathbf{E}_m^b(t+1)\big]^{-1}\, \mathbf{b}_m(t+1).$$

**(g) Backward prediction filter update:**
$$\mathbf{K}_m(t+1) = \mathbf{K}_m(t) + \frac{\boldsymbol{\phi}(t+1, m-1)\, \mathbf{b}_m^T(t+1)}{\gamma_{m-1}(t+1)\, \lambda + \boldsymbol{\phi}^T(t+1, m-1)\, \mathbf{R}_{m-1}^{-1}(t)\, \boldsymbol{\phi}(t+1, m-1)}.$$

### 2.10 Joint Process Estimation

The desired output $y(t)$ is estimated using the orthogonal backward prediction error basis. Define the **joint process estimation error** (a scalar) at each lattice stage:

$$\varepsilon_0(t) = y(t),$$

$$\boxed{\varepsilon_m(t) = \varepsilon_{m-1}(t) - \boldsymbol{\rho}_m^T(t-1)\, \mathbf{b}_m(t), \qquad m = 1, \ldots, M,}$$

where $\boldsymbol{\rho}_m(t) \in \mathbb{R}^{\Delta N(m-1)}$ is the **joint process estimation coefficient** (a vector, since $\mathbf{b}_m(t)$ is a vector and $y(t)$ is a scalar):

$$\boldsymbol{\rho}_m(t) = \big[\mathbf{E}_m^b(t)\big]^{-1} \sum_{s=1}^{t} \lambda^{t-s}\, \mathbf{b}_m(s)\, \varepsilon_{m-1}(s).$$

**Time update for the joint process coefficient:**

$$\boxed{\boldsymbol{\rho}_m(t+1) = \boldsymbol{\rho}_m(t) + \frac{\big[\mathbf{E}_m^b(t+1)\big]^{-1}\, \mathbf{b}_m(t+1)\, \varepsilon_m(t+1)}{\gamma_{m-1}(t+1)}.}$$

The **a posteriori estimation error** at order $M$ is:

$$\varepsilon_M(t) = y(t) - \hat{y}_M(t), \qquad \hat{y}_M(t) = \sum_{m=0}^{M} \boldsymbol{\rho}_m^T(t)\, \mathbf{b}_m(t).$$

This is the RLS lattice estimate of the Volterra system output.

### 2.11 Order-Recursive Update of the Parameter Estimate

The order recursion from $M$ to $M+1$ uses the **block matrix inversion** of the partitioned correlation matrix:

$$\mathbf{R}_{M+1}(t) = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{R}_M(t) & \mathbf{r}(t) \\ \mathbf{r}^T(t) & \mathbf{R}_\zeta(t) \end{bmatrix},$$

where $\mathbf{r}(t) = \sum_{s=1}^t \lambda^{t-s} \boldsymbol{\phi}(s,M)\boldsymbol{\zeta}^T(s,M+1)$ and $\mathbf{R}_\zeta(t) = \sum_{s=1}^t \lambda^{t-s} \boldsymbol{\zeta}(s,M+1)\boldsymbol{\zeta}^T(s,M+1)$.

The **Schur complement** gives the backward error energy:

$$\mathbf{E}_{M+1}^b(t) = \mathbf{R}_\zeta(t) - \mathbf{r}^T(t)\, \mathbf{R}_M^{-1}(t)\, \mathbf{r}(t).$$

The inverse is updated via block inversion:

$$\mathbf{R}_{M+1}^{-1}(t) = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{R}_M^{-1}(t) + \mathbf{K}_{M+1}(t)\,\big[\mathbf{E}_{M+1}^b(t)\big]^{-1}\mathbf{K}_{M+1}^T(t) & -\mathbf{K}_{M+1}(t)\,\big[\mathbf{E}_{M+1}^b(t)\big]^{-1} \\ -\

## Part 1: Casting the Volterra System as a Linear Model via Kronecker Tensor Product

### 1.1 Input Vector and Kronecker Products

Define the **input snapshot vector** at time $t$ with memory order $M$:

$$\mathbf{x}(t, M) = \big[x(t),\; x(t-1),\; \ldots,\; x(t-M)\big]^T \in \mathbb{R}^{M+1}.$$

Define the **$k$-fold Kronecker product**:

$$\mathbf{x}^{[k]}(t, M) = \underbrace{\mathbf{x}(t,M) \otimes \mathbf{x}(t,M) \otimes \cdots \otimes \mathbf{x}(t,M)}_{k \text{ times}} \in \mathbb{R}^{(M+1)^k}.$$

By the definition of the Kronecker product, the entry of $\mathbf{x}^{[k]}(t,M)$ at the position indexed by the multi-index $(t_1, t_2, \ldots, t_k)$ with $t_i \in \{0, 1, \ldots, M\}$ is exactly

$$\big[\mathbf{x}^{[k]}(t,M)\big]_{(t_1,\ldots,t_k)} = \prod_{i=1}^{k} x(t - t_i).$$

### 1.2 Vectorizing the Volterra Kernel

Define $\mathbf{h}_{M,k} \in \mathbb{R}^{(M+1)^k}$ as the **vectorized $k$-th order Volterra kernel**, whose entries are $h_k(t_1, \ldots, t_k)$ arranged in the **same lexicographic order** as the entries of $\mathbf{x}^{[k]}(t, M)$. Then the $k$-th order Volterra contribution becomes an inner product:

$$\sum_{t_1, \ldots, t_k = 0}^{M} h_k(t_1, \ldots, t_k) \prod_{i=1}^{k} x(t - t_i) = \big[\mathbf{x}^{[k]}(t, M)\big]^T \mathbf{h}_{M,k}.$$

### 1.3 Assembling the Linear Model

Define the **data row vector** for the $k$-th order term:

$$\mathbf{D}_x(t, k, M) = \big[\mathbf{x}^{[k]}(t, M)\big]^T \in \mathbb{R}^{1 \times (M+1)^k}.$$

Stacking all $p$ orders, define the **combined parameter vector** and **combined data row vector**:

$$\mathbf{g}_M = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{h}_{M,1} \\ \mathbf{h}_{M,2} \\ \vdots \\ \mathbf{h}_{M,p} \end{bmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^{N(M)}, \qquad \mathbf{D}_x(t, M) = \big[\mathbf{D}_x(t,1,M),\; \ldots,\; \mathbf{D}_x(t,p,M)\big] \in \mathbb{R}^{1 \times N(M)},$$

where $N(M) = \sum_{k=1}^{p} (M+1)^k$ is the total number of parameters.

Collecting data over $s = 1, \ldots, t$, the **batch data matrix** is:

$$\mathbf{D}_x(t, M) = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{D}_x(1, M) \\ \mathbf{D}_x(2, M) \\ \vdots \\ \mathbf{D}_x(t, M) \end{bmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^{t \times N(M)}, \qquad \mathbf{y}_t = \begin{bmatrix} y(1) \\ \vdots \\ y(t) \end{bmatrix}, \quad \mathbf{e}_t = \begin{bmatrix} e(1) \\ \vdots \\ e(t) \end{bmatrix}.$$

The Volterra system is now cast as the **linear regression model**:

$$\boxed{\mathbf{y}_t = \mathbf{D}_x(t, M)\, \mathbf{g}_M + \mathbf{e}_t.}$$

Equivalently, at each time instant:

$$y(t) = \boldsymbol{\phi}^T(t, M)\, \mathbf{g}_M + e(t),$$

where $\boldsymbol{\phi}(t, M) = \mathbf{D}_x^T(t, M) = \big[\mathbf{x}^{[1]}(t,M)^T, \ldots, \mathbf{x}^{[p]}(t,M)^T\big]^T \in \mathbb{R}^{N(M)}$ is the **regressor vector**.

## Part 2: RLS Lattice Algorithm for Estimating $\mathbf{g}_M$

### 2.1 RLS Cost Function

The RLS estimate at time $t$, memory order $M$, minimizes the exponentially weighted least-squares cost:

$$J(t, M) = \sum_{s=1}^{t} \lambda^{t-s} \big[y(s) - \boldsymbol{\phi}^T(s, M)\, \hat{\mathbf{g}}_M(t)\big]^2, \qquad 0 < \lambda \leq 1,$$

where $\lambda$ is the **forgetting factor**. The solution is:

$$\hat{\mathbf{g}}_M(t) = \mathbf{R}_M^{-1}(t)\, \mathbf{p}_M(t),$$

with $\mathbf{R}_M(t) = \sum_{s=1}^{t} \lambda^{t-s} \boldsymbol{\phi}(s,M)\boldsymbol{\phi}^T(s,M)$ and $\mathbf{p}_M(t) = \sum_{s=1}^{t} \lambda^{t-s} \boldsymbol{\phi}(s,M)\, y(s)$.

### 2.2 Nested (Order-Recursive) Structure of the Regressor

The key property enabling the lattice is the **nested structure**: when $M \to M+1$, the input vector gains one component $x(t-M-1)$, and the Kronecker products grow accordingly. Specifically:

$$\mathbf{x}(t, M+1) = \big[\mathbf{x}(t,M)^T,\; x(t-M-1)\big]^T,$$

and the regressor decomposes as:

$$\boldsymbol{\phi}(t, M+1) = \begin{bmatrix} \boldsymbol{\phi}(t, M) \\ \boldsymbol{\zeta}(t, M+1) \end{bmatrix},$$

where $\boldsymbol{\zeta}(t, M+1) \in \mathbb{R}^{\Delta N(M)}$ collects **all new Kronecker product terms** involving $x(t-M-1)$. For each $k = 1, \ldots, p$, the new terms in $\mathbf{x}^{[k]}(t, M+1)$ are those products $\prod_{i=1}^k x(t - t_i)$ where at least one $t_i = M+1$. The dimension of the new block is:

$$\Delta N(M) = N(M+1) - N(M) = \sum_{k=1}^{p} \big[(M+2)^k - (M+1)^k\big].$$

$$\mathbf{b}_m(t) = \boldsymbol{\zeta}(t, m) - \mathbf{K}_m^T(t-1)\, \boldsymbol{\phi}(t, m-1) \in \mathbb{R}^{\Delta N(m-1)},$$

where $\mathbf{K}_m(t) \in \mathbb{R}^{N(m-1) \times \Delta N(m-1)}$ is the **backward prediction filter**:

$$\mathbf{K}_m(t) = \mathbf{R}_{m-1}^{-1}(t) \sum_{s=1}^{t} \lambda^{t-s} \boldsymbol{\phi}(s, m-1)\, \boldsymbol{\zeta}^T(s, m).$$

For the base case ($m = 0$): $\mathbf{b}_0(t) = \boldsymbol{\phi}(t, 0) = \big[x(t), x(t)^2, \ldots, x(t)^p\big]^T \in \mathbb{R}^p$.

**Orthogonality Property.** By construction (Gram–Schmidt orthogonalization in the exponentially weighted inner product $\langle \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \rangle_t = \sum_{s=1}^t \lambda^{t-s} \mathbf{u}^T(s) \mathbf{v}(s)$), the backward prediction errors satisfy:

$$\sum_{s=1}^{t} \lambda^{t-s}\, \mathbf{b}_i(s)\, \mathbf{b}_j^T(s) = \mathbf{0}, \qquad i \neq j.$$

Thus $\{\mathbf{b}_0(t), \mathbf{b}_1(t), \ldots, \mathbf{b}_M(t)\}$ forms an **orthogonal basis** for the column space of $\mathbf{D}_x(t, M)$.

### 2.4 Forward Prediction Errors

$$\mathbf{f}_m(t) = \boldsymbol{\zeta}(t, m) - \mathbf{A}_m^T(t-1)\, \boldsymbol{\phi}(t-1, m-1) \in \mathbb{R}^{\Delta N(m-1)},$$

where $\mathbf{A}_m(t)$ is the **forward prediction filter**:

$$\mathbf{A}_m(t) = \mathbf{R}_{m-1}^{-1}(t-1) \sum_{s=1}^{t} \lambda^{t-s} \boldsymbol{\phi}(s-1, m-1)\, \boldsymbol{\zeta}^T(s, m).$$

### 2.5 Error Energy Matrices and Cross-Correlation

Define the **backward error energy matrix**:

$$\mathbf{E}_m^b(t) = \sum_{s=1}^{t} \lambda^{t-s}\, \mathbf{b}_m(s)\, \mathbf{b}_m^T(s) \in \mathbb{R}^{\Delta N(m-1) \times \Delta N(m-1)}.$$

Define the **forward error energy matrix**:

$$\mathbf{E}_m^f(t) = \sum_{s=1}^{t} \lambda^{t-s}\, \mathbf{f}_m(s)\, \mathbf{f}_m^T(s).$$

Define the **cross-correlation matrix** (capturing the temporal shift relationship):

$$\boldsymbol{\Delta}_m(t) = \sum_{s=1}^{t} \lambda^{t-s}\, \mathbf{f}_{m-1}(s)\, \mathbf{b}_{m-1}^T(s-1).$$
